traditions/methodist/summary: A renewal movement within the Church of England led by John and Charles Wesley, which after Aldersgate (1738) and the start of field preaching (1739) organised converts into societies, classes and bands. American Methodists formed the Methodist Episcopal Church in 1784, and British Methodism separated from the Church of England after Wesley's death (1791). Methodism grew explosively on the American frontier and through mission in Africa, the Pacific and Asia. The United Methodist Church experienced a major schism over sexuality in 2019–2024.
traditions/methodist/distinctives/1: Assurance of salvation through the witness of the Spirit
traditions/methodist/distinctives/2: Christian perfection (entire sanctification) as a goal
traditions/methodist/profile/authority: Scripture as primary, read with tradition, reason and experience (the so-called Wesleyan Quadrilateral); Wesley's Sermons and Notes and the Articles of Religion as doctrinal standards.
traditions/methodist/profile/salvation: God's grace precedes, justifies and sanctifies; all may be saved, and believers can receive assurance and grow toward perfect love.
traditions/methodist/profile/sacraments: Baptism (including infants) and the Lord's Supper as means of grace; Wesley urged frequent communion.
traditions/methodist/profile/eschatology: Classical hope of Christ's return and judgment; nineteenth-century Methodism was often postmillennial and reform-minded.
traditions/methodist/profile/governance: Connexional: conferences appoint itinerant ministers; episcopal in American Methodism, conference-led in British Methodism.
traditions/methodist/profile/worship: Services of preaching and hymn singing with liturgy derived from the Book of Common Prayer; lovefeasts and watchnight services.
traditions/methodist/status: Active; c. 80 million in World Methodist Council member churches (2020).
traditions/holiness-movement/summary: A nineteenth-century revival of Wesley's teaching on entire sanctification, popularised by Phoebe Palmer's Tuesday Meetings (from 1835) and camp meetings after the Civil War. Holiness preachers taught a definite 'second blessing' of heart purity after conversion, often called the baptism of the Holy Spirit. Tensions with mainstream Methodism led to new denominations such as the Wesleyan Methodists, Free Methodists, Church of the Nazarene (1908) and Church of God (Anderson); the movement directly prepared the ground for Pentecostalism.
traditions/holiness-movement/distinctive: Entire sanctification as a second, instantaneous work of grace
'Altar theology' of consecration and faith (Phoebe Palmer)
traditions/holiness-movement/profile/aut: Scripture, read through Wesleyan theology and confirmed in experience.
traditions/holiness-movement/profile/sal: Justification by faith followed by a second definite experience of entire sanctification that cleanses the heart from inbred sin.
traditions/holiness-movement/profile/sac: Baptism and the Lord's Supper, often with flexibility on mode; less sacramental emphasis than early Methodism.
traditions/holiness-movement/profile/esc: Initially postmillennial; many later Holiness groups adopted premillennialism.
traditions/holiness-movement/profile/gov: Varied: episcopal, connexional or congregational denominations.
traditions/holiness-movement/profile/wor: Revivalist services with testimonies, altar calls and gospel songs.
traditions/holiness-movement/status: Active in denominations such as the Church of the Nazarene (c. 2.6 million members) and the Free Methodist and Wesleyan churches.
traditions/salvation-army/summary: Founded in London's East End in 1865 by William and Catherine Booth as the Christian Mission, renamed The Salvation Army in 1878 with a military structure of officers and soldiers. It combines Holiness evangelism with extensive social work among the poor, the homeless and addicts. It does not practise sacraments, believing them non-essential to salvation. Present in over 130 countries, it is one of the world's largest charitable organisations.
traditions/salvation-army/distinctives/1: No sacraments of baptism or communion
traditions/salvation-army/distinctives/3: Women officers and preachers from the outset
traditions/salvation-army/distinctives/4: Large-scale social services and disaster relief
traditions/salvation-army/profile/author: Scripture and the Army's eleven Articles of Faith.
traditions/salvation-army/profile/salvat: Repentance toward God, faith in Christ and regeneration by the Holy Spirit, followed by the privilege of entire sanctification.
traditions/salvation-army/profile/sacram: No outward sacraments; soldiers are enrolled under the flag and emphasise an inward, sacramental life.
traditions/salvation-army/profile/eschat: Christ's return, resurrection, judgment and eternal reward or punishment.
traditions/salvation-army/profile/govern: Hierarchical, led by an elected General and commissioned officers.
traditions/salvation-army/profile/worshi: Informal meetings with brass bands, songs, testimonies and a 'mercy seat' for prayer.
traditions/salvation-army/status: Active; c. 1.5 million soldiers and adherents in over 130 countries.
traditions/evangelical/summary: A transdenominational Protestant movement that emerged from the eighteenth-century awakenings of Edwards, Whitefield and Wesley. David Bebbington characterises it by conversionism, activism, biblicism and crucicentrism. Evangelicals drove missions, abolition and social reform in the nineteenth century; in the twentieth, figures such as Billy Graham and John Stott and the Lausanne Movement (1974) shaped a global identity distinct from fundamentalism. It now spans denominations and independent churches worldwide, with most adherents in the Global South.
traditions/evangelical/distinctives/0: Conversionism: the need for personal conversion
traditions/evangelical/distinctives/1: Biblicism: high regard for the Bible's authority
traditions/evangelical/distinctives/2: Crucicentrism: focus on Christ's atoning death
traditions/evangelical/distinctives/4: Parachurch organisations and global mission networks
traditions/evangelical/profile/authority: The Bible as the inspired and authoritative (often 'inerrant' or 'infallible') Word of God.
traditions/evangelical/profile/salvation: Salvation by grace through personal faith in Christ's substitutionary atonement, usually experienced as being 'born again'.
traditions/evangelical/profile/sacrament: Varies by denomination: infant or believer's baptism; the Lord's Supper commonly seen as memorial or spiritual presence.
traditions/evangelical/profile/eschatolo: Diverse; premillennialism (including dispensationalism) widespread in North America, amillennialism and postmillennialism elsewhere.
traditions/evangelical/profile/governanc: Denominational polity varies; many independent and nondenominational churches.
traditions/evangelical/profile/worship: Preaching-centred services with contemporary or traditional music; strong emphasis on personal devotion.
traditions/evangelical/status: Active; c. 285 million evangelicals (Pew 2010 estimate); definitions and counts vary widely.
traditions/stone-campbell-restoration/su: An American movement seeking Christian unity by restoring the New Testament church, led by former Presbyterians Barton W. Stone (associated with the Cane Ridge revival, 1801) and Thomas and Alexander Campbell. The Stone 'Christians' and Campbell 'Disciples' united in 1832, rejecting creeds as tests of fellowship. Disputes over instrumental music and missionary societies divided the movement into the Churches of Christ (a cappella), the Christian Churches/Churches of Christ, and the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ).
traditions/stone-campbell-restoration/di: 'No creed but Christ, no book but the Bible'
Restoration of New Testament patterns of church life
Believer's baptism by immersion for the remission of sins
Christian unity as a central goal
traditions/stone-campbell-restoration/pr: The New Testament as the pattern for the church, read with common-sense rationality; creeds rejected as tests of fellowship.
Faith, repentance, confession and baptism by immersion for the forgiveness of sins.
Ordinances: believer's baptism by immersion and weekly communion.
Diverse; early Campbell was postmillennial, many later Churches of Christ amillennial.
Congregational, with elders and deacons; the Disciples have regional and general structures.
Weekly communion at the centre; Churches of Christ sing without instruments.
The 66-book Protestant canon, with stress on the New Testament.
traditions/stone-campbell-restoration/st: Active; c. 5 million members across its three main streams worldwide.
traditions/seventh-day-adventist/summary: A Protestant church that emerged from William Miller's Adventist movement after the Great Disappointment of 1844, when Christ did not return as expected. Led by Joseph Bates, James White and Ellen G. White, whose writings are regarded as inspired counsel, believers adopted the seventh-day Sabbath and a doctrine of Christ's heavenly sanctuary ministry. Organised formally in 1863, it is known for health reform, education and medical mission, and is now one of the most widespread Protestant denominations, with most members in Africa and Latin America. It holds Trinitarian doctrine.
traditions/seventh-day-adventist/distinc: Investigative judgment and the heavenly sanctuary (from 1844)
Conditional immortality and annihilation of the wicked
traditions/seventh-day-adventist/profile: Scripture alone as the standard of faith; Ellen G. White's writings regarded as a continuing, authoritative source of truth subordinate to the Bible.
Salvation by grace through faith in Christ, with obedience to God's commandments, including the Sabbath, as the fruit of faith.
Ordinances of believer's baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper preceded by footwashing.
Historicist premillennialism: Christ's visible return, a millennium in heaven, then final destruction of the wicked and a renewed earth.
Representative: local churches, conferences, unions, divisions and the General Conference.
Sabbath School and divine service on Saturday; quarterly communion with footwashing.
traditions/pentecostal/summary: A movement emphasising the baptism in the Holy Spirit, evidenced by speaking in tongues, and the restoration of spiritual gifts such as healing and prophecy. With roots in the Holiness movement and Charles Parham's teaching (Topeka, 1901), it spread worldwide from William J. Seymour's interracial Azusa Street Revival in Los Angeles (1906–1909); parallel revivals arose in India (Mukti, 1905), Korea, Chile and elsewhere. Pentecostalism grew to become one of the largest Christian movements, especially in Latin America, Africa and Asia.
traditions/pentecostal/distinctives/0: Baptism in the Holy Spirit as an experience subsequent to conversion
traditions/pentecostal/distinctives/4: Strong expectation of Christ's return and urgent evangelism
traditions/pentecostal/profile/authority: Scripture as the inspired Word of God, read in expectation that the experiences of Acts continue today.
traditions/pentecostal/profile/salvation: Salvation by grace through faith in Christ, followed by Spirit baptism for empowerment; 'full gospel' of Christ as Saviour, Sanctifier, Spirit-baptiser, Healer and Coming King.
traditions/pentecostal/profile/sacrament: Ordinances of believer's baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper; footwashing in some churches.
traditions/pentecostal/profile/eschatolo: Mostly premillennial, often dispensational, with intense expectation of Christ's imminent return.
traditions/pentecostal/profile/governanc: Varied: congregational, presbyterian-style fellowships and episcopal denominations.
traditions/pentecostal/profile/worship: Spontaneous, exuberant worship with raised hands, tongues, prophecy, prayer for healing and altar calls.
traditions/pentecostal/status: Active; c. 279 million classical Pentecostals in 2010 (Pew); with charismatics, over 580 million.
traditions/assemblies-of-god/summary: The largest Pentecostal denomination, organised at Hot Springs, Arkansas, in 1914 by ministers seeking cooperation and doctrinal order among independent Pentecostal churches. It adopted the Statement of Fundamental Truths in 1916, affirming the Trinity after the Oneness controversy. Through extensive missions, national Assemblies of God churches grew rapidly, notably in Brazil (where a separate movement began in 1911), Nigeria and South Korea, home of Yoido Full Gospel Church.
traditions/assemblies-of-god/distinctive: Spirit baptism with tongues as initial physical evidence
Cooperative fellowship of self-governing national churches
traditions/assemblies-of-god/profile/aut: The Scriptures as the inspired, infallible and authoritative Word of God.
traditions/assemblies-of-god/profile/sal: Salvation by grace through repentance and faith in Christ; Spirit baptism as a distinct subsequent empowerment.
traditions/assemblies-of-god/profile/sac: Ordinances of water baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper.
traditions/assemblies-of-god/profile/esc: Premillennial, with the imminent rapture of the church, Christ's millennial reign and final judgment.
traditions/assemblies-of-god/profile/gov: Cooperative: congregational local churches in district councils and national General Councils, linked by the World Assemblies of God Fellowship.
traditions/assemblies-of-god/profile/wor: Pentecostal worship with contemporary music, spiritual gifts and prayer for healing.
traditions/assemblies-of-god/status: Active; c. 69 million adherents worldwide (World Assemblies of God Fellowship estimate).
